title: Breathless on post-operative day four
presentation: A 58-year-old woman on the orthopaedic ward, four days after an elective right total knee arthroplasty, develops sudden dyspnoea and sharp right-sided chest pain that is worse on inspiration. She had walked to the bathroom with a frame ten minutes earlier. Observations: HR 112, BP 128/76, RR 24, SpO2 91% on air, T 37.6 C.

stages.label: History
stages.text: The operation was uncomplicated under spinal anaesthesia. She was prescribed enoxaparin 40 mg daily for thromboprophylaxis, but the chart shows the doses on days 2 and 3 were held for wound ooze, which has since stopped. She does physiotherapy twice a day but otherwise stays in bed. Past history: obesity (BMI 36), hypertension, and a transdermal oestrogen patch for menopausal symptoms that was not stopped before surgery. No previous venous thromboembolism, no cancer, no haemoptysis, no calf pain. Medications: amlodipine, paracetamol, oxycodone as needed, enoxaparin. Pre-operative creatinine 0.8 mg/dL; no contrast allergy. No cough, fever or chest pain before this afternoon.
stages.prompt: What is your differential, and what is your pre-test probability of pulmonary embolism? Show your working.
stages.learner_goal: Build the differential for acute post-operative dyspnoea and formally estimate PE probability with a validated score before choosing a test.

stages.label: Exam
stages.text: HR 110 regular, BP 126/74, RR 24, SpO2 91% on air rising to 95% on 2 L by nasal cannula. Alert, anxious, speaking in full sentences. Chest clear with no wheeze, crackles or dullness. Heart sounds normal, no loud P2, JVP not elevated. Right knee has the expected post-surgical swelling under a clean dressing; the right calf is slightly larger than the left and mildly tender, which the ward team has attributed to the surgery. Left calf normal. No peripheral oedema. Abdomen soft.
stages.prompt: Which imaging test do you want, and why that one rather than the alternative? Is there anything you would send first that could spare her the scan?
stages.learner_goal: Choose CTPA over V/Q with explicit reasons, and recognise that D-dimer cannot rule out PE in a post-operative patient with a 'PE likely' Wells score.

available_tests.ecg: Sinus tachycardia 110, no S1Q3T3, no right bundle branch block, no T-wave inversion in V1-V4, no ischaemic change.
available_tests.chest x-ray: Clear lung fields, no consolidation, effusion or pneumothorax. Normal heart size.
available_tests.abg: On room air: pH 7.47, PaCO2 31 mmHg, PaO2 61 mmHg, HCO3 23. Alveolar-arterial gradient widened.
available_tests.d-dimer: D-dimer 2,850 ng/mL FEU (reference under 500). Expected to be raised after major surgery regardless of PE.
available_tests.lower limb ultrasound: Compression ultrasound: non-compressible right popliteal vein with echogenic thrombus extending into the proximal calf veins. Left leg normal.
available_tests.ctpa: CT pulmonary angiogram: filling defects in the right lower lobe segmental and subsegmental arteries and the left lower lobe segmental artery. RV/LV diameter ratio 0.9. No pulmonary infarct, no pneumonia, no effusion.
available_tests.v/q scan: If chosen instead of CTPA: two segmental perfusion defects in the right lower lobe and one in the left lower lobe with normal ventilation; high probability. Interpretable only because the chest radiograph is clear.

stages.label: Imaging
stages.text: CT pulmonary angiogram shows filling defects in the right lower lobe segmental and subsegmental arteries and a left lower lobe segmental artery, RV/LV ratio 0.9, no infarct and no alternative diagnosis. High-sensitivity troponin T 24 ng/L, NT-proBNP 480. Compression ultrasound: right popliteal vein thrombus. She remains at HR 108, BP 124/74, SpO2 95% on 2 L.
stages.prompt: Commit. Where does she sit on the PE risk spectrum, what anticoagulant do you start and when, and is there anything you would specifically not do for her tonight?
stages.learner_goal: Risk-stratify a haemodynamically stable PE using RV size and biomarkers, start therapeutic anticoagulation in discussion with the surgical team, and withhold thrombolysis.

diagnosis: Acute pulmonary embolism, provoked (post-operative), intermediate-low risk
key_clues: Sudden pleuritic chest pain and dyspnoea four days after knee arthroplasty with two missed prophylaxis doses
Tachycardia, hypoxaemia and a widened A-a gradient with a clear chest radiograph
Wells score in the 'PE likely' range (6 to 9 depending on how the operated leg is scored)
Asymmetric calf with popliteal vein thrombus on ultrasound
Filling defects on CTPA with RV/LV ratio under 1.0 and only mildly raised troponin
Obesity and transdermal oestrogen as additional risk factors

distractors.name: Hospital-acquired or aspiration pneumonia
distractors.why_not: No cough or sputum, no consolidation on radiograph or CT, and the onset was abrupt.

distractors.name: Post-operative atelectasis
distractors.why_not: Chest is clear and the radiograph shows no volume loss; atelectasis rarely causes this degree of tachycardia and pleuritic pain.

distractors.name: Acute coronary syndrome
distractors.why_not: Pain is pleuritic, ECG shows only sinus tachycardia, and the mild troponin rise is explained by right ventricular strain.

distractors.name: Fat embolism syndrome
distractors.why_not: Typically 24-72 hours after long-bone or arthroplasty surgery with petechiae, confusion and diffuse infiltrates; none are present and the CT is clear apart from emboli.

distractors.name: Pneumothorax
distractors.why_not: Excluded on chest radiograph and CT.

distractors.name: Opioid-related hypoventilation
distractors.why_not: She is alert and tachypnoeic with a low PaCO2, not hypoventilating.

rubric.description: Names pulmonary embolism at the top of the differential
rubric.concept: Sudden dyspnoea and tachycardia in a post-operative patient is PE until proven otherwise

rubric.description: Estimates pre-test probability with Wells (or Geneva) before choosing a test
rubric.concept: Wells score: PE likely (over 4) goes straight to imaging; PE unlikely can be excluded with D-dimer

rubric.description: Recognises that D-dimer cannot rule out PE here (post-operative and 'PE likely'), so goes straight to imaging
rubric.concept: D-dimer only rules out PE in low or unlikely probability; it is nearly always raised after surgery

rubric.description: Orders CT pulmonary angiography as the definitive test
rubric.concept: CTPA is the first-line imaging test for suspected PE in most patients

rubric.description: Explains when V/Q would be preferred (contrast allergy, renal impairment, pregnancy) or that it needs a clear chest radiograph
rubric.concept: V/Q scan is preferred when contrast is contraindicated and the chest radiograph is clear

rubric.description: Risk-stratifies the PE using haemodynamics, troponin or BNP, RV size, or sPESI
rubric.concept: PE severity: shock, RV dysfunction and biomarkers separate high, intermediate and low risk

rubric.description: Starts therapeutic anticoagulation (LMWH initially, transitioning to a DOAC)
rubric.concept: Therapeutic anticoagulation is the treatment for haemodynamically stable PE; LMWH is preferred early after surgery

rubric.description: Withholds thrombolysis in a stable patient four days after major surgery, involves the surgical team, and sets a three-month course for a provoked PE
rubric.concept: Thrombolysis is reserved for high-risk PE; recent major surgery is a contraindication; provoked PE is treated for three months

management_summary: She is haemodynamically stable with a mildly raised troponin and an RV/LV ratio under 1.0: intermediate-low risk (sPESI 1 for heart rate). Start therapeutic anticoagulation tonight with enoxaparin 1 mg/kg twice daily after confirming with the orthopaedic team that the wound is dry; switch to apixaban or rivaroxaban once surgical bleeding risk is acceptable, and treat for three months as a provoked event. No thrombolysis: she is not in shock and major surgery four days ago is a contraindication, so monitor on telemetry with a low threshold for escalation if she deteriorates. Stop the oestrogen patch. Continue mobilisation.
teaching_points: Estimate pre-test probability before you test. Wells 'PE likely' (over 4) means image; D-dimer is only for ruling PE out in 'unlikely' patients, and after major surgery it will be raised regardless, so it costs time without changing the decision.

CTPA is the default: fast, shows alternative diagnoses and RV size. V/Q is the better choice when contrast is the problem (allergy, eGFR under 30), in pregnancy or young women where breast dose matters, and it reads well only with a clear chest radiograph. A positive leg ultrasound in a symptomatic patient can also justify treatment without lung imaging.

Risk-stratify every PE: shock defines high risk; sPESI, troponin and RV size separate intermediate-high from intermediate-low. Intermediate-risk patients are anticoagulated and monitored, not lysed (PEITHO showed bleeding outweighed benefit).
Recent surgery changes the anticoagulant conversation: parenteral LMWH is short-acting and the surgeon should know, and a provoked PE needs three months of treatment, not lifelong.
references: Konstantinides SV et al. 2019 ESC Guidelines for the diagnosis and management of acute pulmonary embolism. Eur Heart J 2020;41:543-603
Wells PS et al. Derivation of a simple clinical model to categorize patients probability of pulmonary embolism: increasing the models utility with the SimpliRED D-dimer. Thromb Haemost 2000;83:416-20
Stein PD et al. Multidetector computed tomography for acute pulmonary embolism (PIOPED II). N Engl J Med 2006;354:2317-27
